opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most underrated things a designer can do right now. When you're designing for AI, the model *is* the material. Traditionally a designer knows their medium really well, whether that's pixels, typography, or interaction patterns, and they understand what's possible and what breaks. With language models, a lot of the product's behavior lives inside the model itself, and you can't get an intuition for that from a spec or a Figma file. You have to sit with it and poke at it.

When you spend real time prompting, trying weird edge cases, and seeing where the model is surprisingly good or confidently wrong, you start to develop a feel for its personality and its failure modes. That changes what you design. You stop drawing a perfect happy-path chat interface and start asking: what happens when the model is uncertain? How do we show that? When should the user be able to steer, edit, or interrupt? Those questions only come up when you've watched the model do unexpected things.

There's also a creative side. A lot of the most interesting interaction ideas came from people noticing an emergent capability and thinking, "Oh, this could be a whole new way of working," rather than bolting AI onto an existing workflow. Designers are really good at spotting those moments, but only if they're close enough to the raw capability to see them.

And I'd say the line between designing and building is blurring. Prototyping directly with the model, writing the prompts, shaping the behavior, even helping make evaluation sets for what "good" looks like, is increasingly part of design. The designers who get their hands dirty with the models end up shaping not just the interface but how the model actually behaves, and that's where a lot of the leverage is now.

r001.rationale: The response says that experimenting with models can reveal emergent capabilities that inspire new interaction ideas and ways of working.

r002.rationale: It discusses designers spotting creative opportunities, but does not say human creativity is a bottleneck to fundamentally reimagining software.

r003.rationale: It mentions prompting and shaping model behavior, but does not state that models can be trained specifically for a product’s intended functionality.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you can't design for something you don't have intuitions about, and the only way to build intuitions about these models is to actually spend hours with them. Not reading about them, not looking at demos, but sitting there and poking at the thing. Asking it weird questions, trying to break it, noticing where it surprises you and where it falls flat.

When I was doing research at Anthropic and then working on product, the most useful insights almost never came from a paper or an eval. They came from this very tactile sense of, oh, the model does this strange thing when you phrase it that way, or it's actually much better at this task than anyone assumed. And that kind of knowledge is exactly what a designer needs, because design is about shaping what the user experiences, and here the material you're shaping is the model's behavior itself.

The traditional design process assumes a fairly deterministic medium. You design a button, it does one thing. With models, the medium is probabilistic and has this huge latent capability surface that nobody fully understands, including the people who trained it. So if you just take the model as a black box API and design a chat window around it, you're leaving most of the interesting design space untouched. A lot of what makes a product feel magical is finding a capability the model has and then building the right affordance so people actually discover it.

I also think there's an inversion happening. Historically, the engineer figured out what was technically possible and the designer made it usable. Now the question of what's possible is itself partly a design question, because it depends on how you prompt, how you set up the interaction, what context you give the model. So designers who play with models end up doing a kind of research. They're discovering behaviors.

And frankly, it's fun. The models are strange and creative in ways that reward curiosity. I'd tell any designer to treat it like learning a new material, the way you'd learn how wood or clay behaves. You have to get your hands on it.

r001.rationale: It says hands-on experimentation reveals model capabilities and surprises that designers can turn into product affordances, generating new design possibilities.

r002.rationale: It discusses designers discovering model behaviors, but does not identify human creativity as a bottleneck to fundamentally reimagining software.

r003.rationale: It discusses prompting and interaction setup, but does not say models can be trained specifically for a product’s intended functionality.

astra-6.text:
I think playing with the models gives you an intuition for what they can actually do. As a designer, you need to understand the material you’re working with. With AI, that means trying things, seeing where the model surprises you, and noticing where it breaks.

That exploration can change what you decide to build. You might start with a familiar interface and then realize the model makes an entirely different interaction possible. Or you might discover that something that looks great in a mockup is unreliable in practice. Spending time with the model helps you design around those capabilities and limitations, instead of making assumptions about them.

r001.rationale: The response says exploration can reveal different interactions and change what a designer builds, but does not clearly state that experimenting generates ideas for new product designs.

r002.rationale: It does not identify human creativity as a bottleneck to fundamentally reimagining software.

r003.rationale: It does not state that AI models can be trained for a product’s intended functionality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think playing with models gives designers an intuition for what they can actually do. You can read about a capability, but it’s different when you try something, get a surprising result, and start asking, “Could this become an interaction? Could I help someone do something they couldn’t do before?”

And you learn where the model breaks. That’s part of the design material, too. If you understand what’s reliable, what’s unpredictable, and where people need control, you can make much better decisions about the experience. So I’d encourage designers to experiment early, before they’ve settled on what the product should look like.

r001.rationale: It says experimenting can lead designers to ask whether a surprising capability could become an interaction or help someone do something new, communicating idea generation for product design.

r002.rationale: It discusses designers learning model capabilities and limitations, but does not identify human creativity as a bottleneck to reimagining software.

r003.rationale: It does not state that models can be trained specifically for a product’s intended functionality.
